--- title: "Take-home Exercise 1 | Public Good" subtitle: "In this take-home exercise, we are interested to investigate the spatial and spatio-temporal patterns of new businesses and firms established in Singapore for the first six months of 2025." date: "Sep 13, 2025" date-modified: "last-modified" author: Linh Nguyen execute: echo: true eval: true freeze: auto message: false warning: false format: html: code-link: true # Clickable function links toc: true # Table of contents code-fold: true # Foldable code code-tools: true # Code tools menu number-sections: true number-offset: 1 editor: visual --- ## Overview ### Objectives - To identify where and when new businesses are established in Singapore, revealing clusters, patterns, and trends - To uncover complex relationships in how new businesses are distributed across the island ### Analysis Questions - What spatial distribution patterns do different business types exhibit across Singapore? - How do survival rates vary between business categories and specific SSIC codes? - Which business types show clustering behavior versus random spatial distribution? - What factors influence business location density and geographic concentration patterns? ### The Data | Dataset | Description | Source | Format | |--------------|------------------|---------------------------|--------------| | **ACRA Information on Corporate Entities** | Information of registered entities in Singapore, including location data | [data.gov.sg](https://data.gov.sg/datasets?query=ACRA+Information+on+Corporate+Entities&page=1&resultId=2) | CSV | | **SSIC: Singapore Standard Industrial Classification 2020** | List of codes represented economic activity of business establishments in Singapore, 2020 version. | [SSIC: Singapore Standard Industrial Classification](https://classification.codes/classifications/industry/ssic-singapore) | Excel | | **MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML** | Polygon data with URA 2019 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundaries | [data.gov.sg](https://data.gov.sg/datasets?query=Master+Plan+Planning+Subzone+boundaries&page=1&resultId=d_6c6d7361dd826d97b91bac914ca6b2ac) | KML | ## Set up R environment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Import R Packages"} pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, tmap, httr, readxl, dplyr, stringr, rvest, knitr, spatstat, terra, raster, sparr, tidyr, kableExtra, ggplot2) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Set seed for Monte Carlo simulations later"} set.seed(1234) ``` ::: ## Data Import & Preparation ### ACRA Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Import ACRA data"} folder_path <- "data/aspatial/ACRA" file_list <- list.files(path = folder_path, pattern = "^ACRA*.*\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) acra_data <- file_list %>% map_dfr(read_csv) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: #### Extracting data of chosen business types The chosen business types are: - SSIC 561: Restaurants, Cafes, Food Courts, Food Kiosks And Bars - SSIC 471: Retail Sale in Non-Specialised Stores - SSIC 681: Real Estate Activities With Own Or Leased Property Details as the following table: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
SSIC Classification Structure for Analysis
SSIC 3-digit prefix Description Alias for this analysis SSIC 4-digit sub-types SSIC 5-digit sub-types
Retail (471)
471 Retail Sale in Non-Specialised Stores **Retail** 4710: Retail Sale in Non-Specialised Stores 47101: Supermarkets and hypermarkets
47102: Mini-marts, convenience stores and provision shops
47103: Department stores
47104: Retail sale in other non-specialised stores n.e.c.
Food & Beverage (561)
561 Restaurants, Cafes, Food Courts, Food Kiosks And Bars **Food & Beverage** 5611: Restaurants and Cafes 56111: Restaurants
5612: Fast Food Outlets, Food Courts and Food Kiosks 56112: Cafes
5613: Pubs 56121: Fast food outlets
5614: Stalls Selling Cooked Food and Prepared Drinks 56122: Food courts, coffee shops and canteens (with mainly food and beverage income)
56123: Food kiosks mainly for takeaway and delivery
56130: Pubs
56140: Stalls Selling Cooked Food and Prepared Drinks
Real Estate (681)
681 Real Estate Activities With Own Or Leased Property **Real Estate** 6810: Real Estate Activities With Own Or Leased Property 68101: Real estate developers
68102: Operating of serviced apartments
68103: Letting of self-owned or leased real estate property except food courts, coffee shops and canteens
68104: Letting and operating of self-owned or leased food courts, coffee shops and canteens
68105: Collective portfolio investment funds with rental income
68106: Management of self-owned strata titled property (i.e. Management Corporation Strata Title)
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Extracting data of chosen business types"} biz_selected <- acra_data %>% select(1:24) %>% filter(str_detect(primary_ssic_code, "^(561|471|681)")) %>% rename(date = registration_incorporation_date) %>% mutate(date = as.Date(date), YEAR = year(date), MONTH_NUM = month(date), MONTH_ABBR = month(date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE)) %>% mutate( postal_code = str_pad(postal_code, width = 6, side = "left", pad = "0")) %>% filter(YEAR >= 2024 & YEAR <= 2025) %>% filter(date >= as.Date("2024-01-01") & date <= as.Date("2025-06-30")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ### SSIC Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Read the Excel file"} ssic_data <- read_excel("data/ssic2020-classification-structure.xlsx", sheet = "SSIC 2020 Structure", skip = 4) # Skip the header rows # Clean the data - remove any rows where SSIC 2020 is NA ssic_data <- ssic_data %>% filter(!is.na(`SSIC 2020`)) # Filter to get only level 5 codes (5-character codes) level5_data <- ssic_data %>% filter(str_length(`SSIC 2020`) == 5) # Create the hierarchy columns ssic_hierarchy <- level5_data %>% mutate( # Level 2: First 2 characters (2-digit number) level_2 = str_sub(`SSIC 2020`, 1, 2), # Level 3: First 3 characters (3-digit number) level_3 = str_sub(`SSIC 2020`, 1, 3), # Level 4: First 4 characters (4-digit number) level_4 = str_sub(`SSIC 2020`, 1, 4), # Level 5: Full 5-character code level_5 = `SSIC 2020`, # Keep the title for reference level_5_description = `SSIC 2020 Title` ) %>% dplyr::select(level_2, level_3, level_4, level_5, level_5_description) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Add the descriptions for each level by joining with the original data"} # Create lookup tables for each level level_2_lookup <- ssic_data %>% filter(str_length(`SSIC 2020`) == 2) %>% dplyr::select(level_2 = `SSIC 2020`, level_2_description = `SSIC 2020 Title`) level_3_lookup <- ssic_data %>% filter(str_length(`SSIC 2020`) == 3) %>% dplyr::select(level_3 = `SSIC 2020`, level_3_description = `SSIC 2020 Title`) level_4_lookup <- ssic_data %>% filter(str_length(`SSIC 2020`) == 4) %>% dplyr::select(level_4 = `SSIC 2020`, level_4_description = `SSIC 2020 Title`) # Join all the descriptions ssic_final <- ssic_hierarchy %>% left_join(level_2_lookup, by = "level_2") %>% left_join(level_3_lookup, by = "level_3") %>% left_join(level_4_lookup, by = "level_4") %>% dplyr::select(level_2, level_2_description, level_3, level_3_description, level_4, level_4_description, level_5, level_5_description) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Join ACRA and SSIC Data"} # Left join ssic_final to biz_selected # Convert primary_ssic_code to character and pad with leading zeros if needed biz_with_hierarchy <- biz_selected %>% mutate(primary_ssic_code = sprintf("%05d", primary_ssic_code)) %>% # Ensures 5-digit format left_join(ssic_final, by = c("primary_ssic_code" = "level_5")) # Check the result str(biz_with_hierarchy) head(biz_with_hierarchy) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ### Geospatial data The Master Plan 2019 Boundary (No Sea) (KML) was downloaded from data.gov.sg that consists of the geographical boundary of Singapore at the planning subzone level. The data is based on URA Master Plan 2019. We will use this to plot the boundaries of the subzones. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Import Singapore Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary dataset"} mpsz <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>% st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>% st_transform(crs = 3414) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Create a function to extract region from KML field"} extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) { if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_) page <- read_html(html_text) rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr") value <- rows %>% keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>% html_element("td") %>% html_text2() if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Extract region from KML field"} mpsz <- mpsz %>% mutate( REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"), PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"), SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"), SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C") ) %>% dplyr::select(-Name, -Description) %>% relocate(geometry, .after = last_col()) mpsz_cl <- mpsz %>% filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP", PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS", PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Geocoding the data"} found <- data.frame() # to store Postal codes that were successfully geocoded with their coordinates not_found <- data.frame(postcode = character()) # to store postal codes that couldn't be matched postcodes <- unique(biz_selected$postal_code) url <- "https://onemap.gov.sg/api/common/elastic/search" for (pc in postcodes) { query <- list( searchVal = pc, returnGeom = "Y", getAddrDetails = "Y", pageNum = "1" ) res <- GET(url, query = query) json <- content(res) if (json$found != 0) { df <- as.data.frame(json$results, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) df$input_postcode <- pc found <- bind_rows(found, df) } else { not_found <- bind_rows(not_found, data.frame(postcode = pc)) } } # Tidying the geocoded data found <- found %>% select(1:10) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Appending the location information"} biz_selected_geocoded = biz_with_hierarchy %>% left_join(found, by = c('postal_code' = 'POSTAL')) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## Data Wrangling ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Create separate datasets for each business type"} # Create separate datasets for each business type to count each type biz_restaurant_cafe <- biz_with_hierarchy %>% filter(str_detect(primary_ssic_code, "^561")) biz_retail_nonspec <- biz_with_hierarchy %>% filter(str_detect(primary_ssic_code, "^471")) biz_real_estate <- biz_with_hierarchy %>% filter(str_detect(primary_ssic_code, "^681")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Before applying the `st_as_sf` function to convert the data into simple point features, we check for missing values first and remove such records. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Converting into simple point features - SF data frame"} biz_with_coords <- biz_selected_geocoded %>% # Remove records without coordinates filter(!is.na(X) & !is.na(Y)) %>% # Convert LATITUDE and LONGITUDE to numeric if they're character mutate( LATITUDE = as.numeric(X), LONGITUDE = as.numeric(Y) ) biz_sf <- st_as_sf(biz_with_coords, coords = c("X","Y"), crs=3414) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Create separate datasets for each business type for later individual analysis"} biz_restaurant_cafe_sf <- biz_sf %>% filter(str_detect(primary_ssic_code, "^561")) biz_retail_nonspec_sf <- biz_sf %>% filter(str_detect(primary_ssic_code, "^471")) biz_real_estate_sf <- biz_sf %>% filter(str_detect(primary_ssic_code, "^681")) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ### Verify the point features ::: panel-tabset #### Retail ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Plot"} plot(st_geometry(biz_retail_nonspec_sf), main = "Business Point Features", pch = 16, cex = 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### Food & Beverages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Plot"} plot(st_geometry(biz_restaurant_cafe_sf), main = "Business Point Features", pch = 16, cex = 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: #### Real Estate ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Plot"} plot(st_geometry(biz_real_estate_sf), main = "Business Point Features", pch = 16, cex = 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: ## Exploratory Data Analysis ::: panel-tabset ### Summary on the chosen business types ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Create a summary table of all the chosen business types using kable"} # Step 1: Create summary table from biz_with_hierarchy with both total and live counts biz_summary <- biz_with_hierarchy %>% group_by(primary_ssic_code) %>% summarise( business_count = n(), live_business_count = sum(entity_status_description == "Live", na.rm = TRUE), live_percentage = round(live_business_count / business_count * 100, 1), .groups = 'drop' ) %>% filter(!is.na(primary_ssic_code)) # Step 2: Join with ssic_final on primary_ssic_code = level_5 biz_hierarchy_summary <- biz_summary %>% left_join(ssic_final, by = c("primary_ssic_code" = "level_5")) # Step 3: Create concatenated descriptions biz_pivot_table <- biz_hierarchy_summary %>% mutate( level_3_concat = paste(level_3, level_3_description, sep = " - "), level_4_concat = paste(level_4, level_4_description, sep = " - "), level_5_concat = paste(primary_ssic_code, level_5_description, sep = " - ") ) %>% arrange(level_3_concat, level_4_concat, level_5_concat) # Step 4: Keep only the columns we need biz_pivot_table <- biz_pivot_table[, c("level_3_concat", "level_4_concat", "level_5_concat", "business_count", "live_business_count", "live_percentage")] # Step 5: Display with kable including the new column biz_pivot_table %>% kable(caption = "Business Distribution by SSIC Hierarchy", col.names = c("Level 3", "Level 4", "Level 5", "Total", "Live", "Live %")) %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>% column_spec(4:6, bold = TRUE) %>% pack_rows(index = table(biz_pivot_table$level_3_concat)) %>% scroll_box(height = "500px") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: Based on the business summary above, we can draw some key insights about business types and survival rates: - **Food & Beverage** dominates with 5,542 businesses (69.1% of total), reflecting Singapore's vibrant food scene but challenging market conditions with 27.4% survival rate - **Traditional food stalls** excel (52.3% survival) vs. restaurants struggle (8% survival), suggesting lower overhead and established customer bases favor traditional formats - **Real estate** sector shows poor resilience with only 6.7% survival rate, likely due to high capital requirements and market volatility affecting property investments - **Retail stores** perform moderately (25.9% survival) with department stores outperforming (43.3%) supermarkets (13.8%), indicating differentiated positioning beats commodity retail - **Overall** 24.4% survival rate suggests high business turnover in Singapore, reflecting competitive market dynamics and regulatory compliance challenges across sectors **Key insight:** Asset-light, established food formats and specialized retail show better survival than capital-intensive businesses. ### Plotting business points on Singapore boundary As the number of business points per business type is large itself, plotting all of them on `mpsz` - Singapore boundary will be too packed and we will not be able to extract any pattern out of it. Therefore, it is a good idea to plot them separately as below. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Plot"} ggplot() + geom_sf(data = mpsz_cl, fill = "lightgray", color = "white") + geom_sf(data = biz_sf, aes(color = as.factor(primary_ssic_code)), size = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) + facet_wrap(~ primary_ssic_code) + # Remove scales = "free" theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "none") + # Hide legend since facets show the codes labs(title = "Business Locations by SSIC Code") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Based on the business location plots, here are key observations about spatial density patterns: **Food & Beverage Sector (Food & Beverages):** - 56111 (Restaurants) and 56140 (Food stalls) show the highest density and widest distribution across Singapore, indicating ubiquitous presence in residential and commercial areas - 56122 (Food courts/coffee shops) displays concentrated clusters, likely in HDB estates and commercial centers where these establishments serve local communities - 56123 (Food kiosks) shows moderate density with scattered distribution, reflecting their mobile/flexible nature - 56112 (Cafes) and 56130 (Pubs) are more selectively located, probably in trendy districts and entertainment areas **Retail Sector (Retail):** - 47109 (Other non-specialised stores) shows broad distribution but lower density than food businesses - 47101-47103 display very sparse, clustered patterns, suggesting these larger retail formats locate in specific commercial zones **Real Estate Sector (Real Estate):** - 68103 (Property letting) shows moderate clustering in business districts Other real estate activities (68101, 68102, 68104-68106) are extremely sparse, reflecting their specialized, capital-intensive nature ::: ## CORE SPATIAL ANALYSIS - REGISTRATION INTENT ANALYSIS ### Spatial KDE Analysis #### Individual Density Surfaces ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Create Owin object"} sg_owin <- as.owin(mpsz_cl) ``` ::: ::: panel-tabset ##### Retail ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Convert sf data frames to ppp class and calculate KDE"} # Convert sf data frames to ppp class ppp_retail_all <- as.ppp(biz_retail_nonspec_sf) ppp_retail_all = ppp_retail_all[sg_owin] # Calculate KDE using spatstat kde_retail_all <- density(ppp_retail_all, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE, kernel="gaussian") plot(kde_retail_all) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The KDE plot reveals Singapore's retail sector exhibits extreme spatial concentration with very low overall density values (maximum 5e-04). Most areas show near-zero density, indicating retail is strategically clustered in specific commercial zones rather than dispersed. Clear hotspots appear in central regions while peripheral areas remain virtually retail-free. This pattern reflects Singapore's controlled urban planning where retail development concentrates in designated commercial nodes, demonstrating the city-state's planned economy approach to spatial development. ##### Food & Beverages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Convert sf data frames to ppp class and calculate KDE"} # Convert sf data frames to ppp class ppp_restaurants_all <- as.ppp(biz_restaurant_cafe_sf) ppp_restaurants_all = ppp_restaurants_all[sg_owin] # Calculate KDE using spatstat kde_restaurants_all <- density(ppp_restaurants_all, sigma = bw.diggle, # Automatic bandwidth selection edge = TRUE, kernel="gaussian") # Edge correction plot(kde_restaurants_all) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The restaurant sector KDE shows significantly higher density values (maximum 0.001) compared to retail (5e-04), indicating roughly double the spatial concentration. Restaurant distribution displays more pronounced central clustering with visible hotspots in what appears to be Singapore's CBD and urban core areas. Unlike retail's extremely sparse pattern, restaurants show moderate density gradients extending from central hotspots. This reflects restaurants' need for high foot traffic and accessibility, leading to denser clustering in commercial and mixed-use districts. The higher overall density suggests restaurants are more ubiquitous across Singapore's urban landscape than retail establishments, likely due to daily dining needs versus less frequent retail shopping patterns. ##### Real Estate ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Convert sf data frames to ppp class and calculate KDE"} # Convert sf data frames to ppp class ppp_realestate_all <- as.ppp(biz_real_estate_sf) ppp_realestate_all = ppp_realestate_all[sg_owin] # Calculate KDE using spatstat kde_realestate_all <- density(ppp_realestate_all, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE, kernel="gaussian") plot(kde_realestate_all) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-home_Ex01_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-38-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The real estate KDE displays the lowest density values among all three sectors (maximum 3e-04), indicating the most sparse and selective spatial distribution. Real estate activities show minimal clustering with only faint hotspots visible in central areas, reflecting the capital-intensive nature and specialized zoning requirements of property development. Compared to restaurants (0.001 density) and retail (5e-04 density), real estate demonstrates the most constrained spatial pattern, likely concentrated in designated commercial and mixed-use zones where property development is permitted. This stark contrast highlights how regulatory frameworks and high capital barriers limit real estate activities to specific strategic locations, unlike the more consumer-driven distribution patterns of restaurants and retail establishments. ::: #### Perform the Clark-Evans test with CSR In this section, we will perform Clark-Evans tests for the 3 business entities separately, to quantify whether a point pattern is clustered, random, or uniformly spaced. The result will help us understand the underlying spatial patterns of each business type. This will inform our interpretation of the subsequent KDE analysis. The confidence level chosen for the test is 95%. Therefore, we can set the number simulation at the minimum of `nsim = 39`. ::: panel-tabset ##### Food & Beverages The test hypotheses are: - Ho = The distribution of Food & Beverages are randomly distributed. - H1 = The distribution of Food & Beverages are not randomly distributed. The 95% confident interval will be used. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Clark-Evans test with Monte Carlo simulations"} clarkevans.test(ppp_restaurants_all, correction="none", clipregion="sg_owin", alternative=c("clustered"), method="MonteCarlo", nsim=39) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Clark-Evans test No edge correction Monte Carlo test based on 39 simulations of CSR with fixed n data: ppp_restaurants_all R = 0.35908, p-value = 0.025 alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1) ``` ::: ::: The Clark-Evans test reveals that restaurants and cafes (SSIC Food & Beverages) in the study area exhibit a significantly clustered spatial distribution (R = 0.35908, p \< 0.05). This strong clustering pattern suggests that food service establishments tend to co-locate rather than distribute randomly across the landscape. The clustering likely reflects agglomeration benefits where restaurants benefit from proximity to competitors through shared customer traffic, as well as urban planning policies that concentrate commercial activities in designated zones. This spatial concentration creates identifiable dining districts and food hubs within the study area, which has important implications for business location strategy and urban commercial planning. ##### Retail The test hypotheses are: - Ho = The distribution of Retail are randomly distributed. - H1 = The distribution of Retail are not randomly distributed. The 95% confident interval will be used. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-summary="Clark-Evans test with Monte Carlo simulations"} clarkevans.test(ppp_retail_all, correction="none", clipregion="sg_owin", alternative=c("clustered"), method="MonteCarlo", nsim=39) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Clark-Evans test No edge correction Monte Carlo test based on 39 simulations of CSR with fixed n data: ppp_retail_all R = 0.45778, p-value = 0.025 alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1) ``` ::: ::: The Clark-Evans test indicates that non-specialised retail stores (SSIC Retail) exhibit a significantly clustered spatial distribution (R = 0.46, p \< 0.05). While still showing clustering behavior, these retail establishments are somewhat more dispersed than restaurants and cafes, reflecting their need to serve broader geographic markets while still benefiting from commercial agglomeration in shopping districts and retail centers. ##### Real Estate The test hypotheses are: - Ho = The distribution of Real Estate are randomly distributed. - H1 = The distribution of Real Estate are not randomly distributed. My approach for this analysis is as follows: - **F-function Analysis**: Measures empty space accessibility from random locations to identify underserved areas - **L-function Analysis**: Detects clustering intensity using the clear above/below envelope interpretation - **Cross L-functions**: Quantify inter-business type spatial interactions to determine attraction, repulsion, or independence between business types - **Combined F-L Analysis**: Provides comprehensive pattern validation through dual complementary perspectives on spatial distribution ### L-Function Analysis I employ L-function analysis for its superior interpretability over K-functions, where deviations above/below the theoretical line clearly indicate clustering or regularity. Interaction_Type 1 Restaurants ↔ Retail ATTRACTION 2 Restaurants ↔ Real Estate ATTRACTION 3 Retail ↔ Real Estate ATTRACTION ``` ::: ::: ## Conclusions and Future Improvements ### Conclusion This comprehensive dual-layer spatial analysis of Singapore's business registration patterns from 2024-2025 provides crucial evidence-based insights for strategic urban land use planning and management. The consistent clustering patterns across restaurants (561), retail (471), and real estate (681) business types, particularly concentrated in Marina Bay and CBD areas, demonstrate the powerful influence of agglomeration economics on business location decisions. The F-function and L-function analyses reveal minimal empty space and strong clustering tendencies in these prime districts, indicating market-driven spatial optimization that urban planners should acknowledge and support rather than resist. The findings advocate for a **multi-tiered commercial development** strategy that balances intensification of successful business ecosystems with strategic decentralization to underserved areas. Marina Bay and CBD's dominance necessitates enhanced mixed-use zoning policies with higher plot ratios and vertical integration requirements to maximize land efficiency while maintaining sustainable density levels. Simultaneously, the identification of excessive empty space in peripheral regions like Yishun, Sembawang, and Pasir Ris presents opportunities for targeted satellite commercial hub development through strategic incentives and infrastructure investments. The cross L-function results demonstrating attraction relationships between business types support integrated commercial corridor development, enabling Singapore to create seamless business ecosystems that leverage synergistic relationships. However, the intense clustering also raises legitimate concerns about market oversaturation, commercial rent inflation, and equitable access to services across the island. Urban planners must implement competition management policies including business diversity quotas and affordable commercial space preservation to maintain market health. The registration intent versus business success comparison reveals that entrepreneur preferences align with viable business locations, suggesting market mechanisms effectively identify optimal commercial areas. This validates a planning approach that works with natural clustering tendencies while proactively developing alternative business districts to ensure sustainable, equitable urban growth. These evidence-based recommendations provide a robust framework for managing Singapore's commercial landscape evolution while maintaining its position as a leading global business hub. ### Acknowledged Limitations for Future Improvements This study presents several methodological limitations that may affect the comprehensiveness of findings. - SSIC aggregation at 3-digit level potentially masks important intra-category spatial variations - for example, fine-dining restaurants (56111) versus fast-food outlets (56112) likely exhibit distinct clustering behaviors that remain undetected in the current 561-level analysis. - Temporal scope limitation to 18 months (Jan 2024-Jun 2025) may not capture long-term cyclical patterns or seasonal business formation trends. - Scale dependency represents another constraint - the analysis focuses on citywide patterns without examining neighborhood-level clustering variations or micro-location factors influencing business success within identified hotspots. ## References Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority.
